Hormah
HOR-muh
proper noun
From the Hebrew chormah, “utter destruction” or “a thing devoted to the ban,” from the root charam, “to devote to destruction.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Hormah is a place whose very name preaches a sermon: “utter destruction.” Its history begins in shame. When Israel, having rebelled at the report of the spies, presumed to go up into the hill country without the LORD and without the ark, the Amalekites and Canaanites came down and smote them, beating them back as far as Hormah. There the name marked Israel’s defeat — not Canaan’s destruction but their own, for they went up in self-will after the LORD had pronounced judgment. Yet the place is redeemed in record by a later and rightly-ordered devotion. When the Canaanite king of Arad fought against Israel, the people vowed a vow unto the LORD: if He would deliver this people into their hand, they would utterly destroy their cities. The LORD hearkened, delivered up the Canaanites, and Israel utterly destroyed them and their cities, and called the name of the place Hormah — the same word now signifying victory under God’s sanction. After the conquest the men of Judah and Simeon smote the inhabitants of Zephath and devoted it likewise. Hormah thus stands as a double witness: destruction visited upon presumptuous Israel, and destruction visited by faithful Israel upon Canaan’s wickedness. The difference is obedience. The same enterprise pursued in self-will brings ruin; pursued in submission to God, it brings the promised inheritance.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A place in the Negeb whose name means “utter destruction,” marking both Israel’s defeat in presumption and Canaan’s devotion to the ban.

expand to see more

HORMAH, a place in the south of Canaan, formerly the Canaanite city of Zephath.

The point to which the Amalekites and Canaanites beat back presumptuous Israel (Num 14:45).

Named Hormah after Israel utterly destroyed the Canaanites in answer to a vow (Num 21:3).

Smitten and devoted by Judah and Simeon in the days of the conquest (Jdg 1:17).

Its name from charam, to devote a thing to destruction under the ban.

📖 Key Scripture

Num 14:45 — "Then the Amalekites came down, and the Canaanites which dwelt in that hill, and smote them, and discomfited them, even unto Hormah."

Num 21:3 — "And the LORD hearkened to the voice of Israel, and delivered up the Canaanites; and they utterly destroyed them and their cities: and he called the name of the place Hormah."

Jdg 1:17 — "And Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they slew the Canaanites that inhabited Zephath, and utterly destroyed it. And the name of the city was called Hormah."

Num 21:2 — "And Israel vowed a vow unto the LORD, and said, If thou wilt indeed deliver this people into my hand, then I will utterly destroy their cities."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The lesson to recover is that the same work brings ruin in self-will and victory in obedience to God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Hormah teaches the difference between presumption and faith. When Israel went up in self-will, contrary to the LORD’s word, the name “utter destruction” fell upon their own heads, and they were beaten back. Zeal that runs ahead of God, undertaking His work without His command or His presence, ends in defeat however earnest its intentions.

The same name afterward crowned a true obedience. When Israel vowed and waited and went up under the LORD’s deliverance, Hormah became a trophy of victory. The believer learns that the worth of any labor lies not in its energy but in its submission to the will of God. To act in faith and at His bidding is to inherit; to act in presumption is to be discomfited even in a good cause.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name comes from charam, to ban or devote to destruction, the same root behind cherem, the accursed thing set apart for ruin.

expand to see more

Hormah — from Hebrew chormah, “utter destruction, devotion to the ban.”

From the root charam, “to devote, to utterly destroy.”

Kin to cherem, the accursed or devoted thing (Jos 7:1).

The former name of the site was Zephath, “watch-tower” (Jdg 1:17).

The name applied to the place after Canaan was put to the ban there (Num 21:3).

Usage

"The presumptuous host was driven back unto Hormah, their defeat sealing the name."

"After the vow was kept, the people called the conquered place Hormah."

"Judah and Simeon devoted Zephath and named the city Hormah anew."
